analysis.one_liner: Repeals the new 15% minimum tax on the profits of very large corporations.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the 15% corporate minimum tax was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2022, Congress created a corporate alternative minimum tax: corporations with more than $1 billion in yearly profits must pay at least 15% of their reported earnings in federal tax, no matter how many deductions and credits they use. This bill would erase that tax, returning those companies to the regular system where accounting deductions can shrink their tax bills. It would also undo the 1% excise tax on corporate stock buybacks that came with the minimum tax. The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Very large profitable corporations — the roughly 100 or so U.S. companies with more than $1 billion in annual income that the minimum tax covers — would pay less in federal taxes and could resume larger stock buybacks free of the 1% excise tax.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the corporate alternative minimum tax enacted in the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, which requires corporations with over $1 billion in annual income to pay at least 15% on reported earnings.
Eliminates the only federal minimum tax on the book income of the largest corporations, letting them resume using deductions and credits to reduce their tax bills toward zero.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would forgo the tax revenue, so the cost would fall on other taxpayers or future deficits; the biggest companies that currently owe the minimum tax would be the direct gainers at their expense.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would eliminate a tax that applies only to corporations with over $1 billion in profits, aimed at ensuring very large profitable companies pay at least some tax even when book income is high.
Repealing the tax would erase the revenue it was projected to raise, adding to federal deficits unless replaced elsewhere.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a large tax cut to a small set of highly profitable corporations, with no offsetting revenue, leaving the cost to be borne through borrowing or future taxes. Its repeal would also remove the limit on buybacks, a modest restraint on corporate stock enriching shareholders. It offered no countervailing benefit to ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It was read once in the Senate and sent to the Finance Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2023 with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 29, 2022 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, and no further action was recorded.
The bill would have repealed the 15% corporate alternative minimum tax created by the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Very large corporations keep paying the 15% minimum tax on their reported profits, and the federal revenue from it remains on the books. Ordinary taxpayers avoided shouldering the cost of the repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations, who keep paying the minimum tax

for.name: Sen. John Barrasso
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the corporate alternative minimum tax.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrats signed on, and the underlying corporate minimum tax had been enacted on party lines in the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022.

industries.industry: Very large profitable corporations (over $1 billion in annual income)
industries.note: The bill repeals the 15% minimum tax on their reported profits, allowing them to lower their effective tax rates through deductions and credits. Only companies above the $1 billion threshold were covered, so the benefit is concentrated among the largest firms.

industries.industry: Private equity and publicly traded companies issuing large stock buybacks
industries.note: The corporate minimum tax includes a 1% excise tax on stock buybacks; repeal would remove it, making buybacks cheaper. Repeal would also unwind revenue that was partly earmarked for drug price negotiation and energy provisions under the same law.
